title: India's Clinical Underdog Will Carry the Healthcare System on Its Back
description: This article examines the structural imbalances in India's public health system, focusing on how secondary care facilities often overlooked in policy design serve as the system's true workhorses. It highlights the significant 'mismatch' between intended patient pathways (which prioritize primary care) and the reality where patients bypass primary facilities in favor of secondary and tertiary care.
author: Pratyush Mohanty

body.raw:
**India's Clinical Underdog Will Carry the Healthcare System on Its Back**

In the architecture of India's public health system, secondary care facilities have long been the unrecognized workhorses. While primary care centers remain the focal point of national health policy and tertiary hospitals command the bulk of specialized investment, it is the secondary tier that quietly absorbs the vast majority of the nation's complex and escalating health demands. These district hospitals and community centers are the clinical underdogs of India \- chronically underfunded, yet generating the most comprehensive, longitudinal clinical data in the subcontinent. To understand how this tier carries the system on its back, one must look past intended policy design and observe the actual paths patients take every day.

### **THE MISMATCH: DESIGN VERSUS REALITY**

*In a district on the outskirts of Bhubaneswar, two patients begin their mornings with different expectations of care. Ramesh leaves early. A schoolteacher in his forties, he has been dealing with a persistent cough for a few days. The Primary Health Centre is close, familiar, and accessible. By mid-morning, he has been seen, prescribed medication, and advised rest. The interaction is brief \- no more than five to seven minutes, consistent with average consultation times in public primary care settings in India (MoHFW, 2022). It is, in many ways, what the system was designed for: early presentation, limited escalation, and minimal intervention.*

*Across the district, Sushila waits longer. A daily wage worker, she has been experiencing fatigue and breathlessness for weeks. The nearest primary facility had no doctor on her last visit \- a reflection of persistent workforce gaps, where vacancy rates for specialists in public facilities can exceed 20–30% in several regions (Rural Health Statistics, 2022). This time, her family arranges transport to the district hospital. By the time she arrives, the outpatient department is already operating at capacity. She waits, is eventually seen, and enters a more complex clinical pathway \- diagnostics, prescriptions, and follow-ups \- each step generating fragments of information that will likely remain disconnected.*

Both patients move through the same system. Only one passes through the part of it that sees what happens when early care does not. What emerges from this contrast is not an exception, but a pattern. Across India, nearly 60–70% of patients bypass primary care and seek treatment directly at secondary or higher-level facilities (NHSRC, 2019). The reasons are not singular. They include perceived quality differences, availability of doctors, prior experience, and the unpredictability of service delivery. What follows is a quiet but sustained shift \- one in which the system’s intended entry point is no longer its functional one. This divergence between intended system design and actual patient behavior is illustrated in Figure 1\.

![][image1]

Figure 1: Mismatch between intended and actual patient flow in India’s healthcare system. While primary care is designed to handle the majority of cases, real-world utilization shows a significant shift toward secondary care, driven by access variability, perceived quality, and provider availability. Source: NHSRC (2019); Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (2022); WHO (2022).

In effect, the architecture remains tiered, but its usage has flattened toward the middle. This has implications that extend beyond congestion. Healthcare systems globally are undergoing a transition \- from episodic encounters to continuous, data-informed care. Electronic health records, interoperable platforms, and predictive analytics have begun to enable this shift, allowing systems to track disease trajectories over time rather than respond to isolated events (WHO, 2022). The underlying premise is straightforward: better data leads to better decisions.

### **THE BOTTLENECK: DATA USABILITY**

India is not outside this trajectory. But it enters it from a different structural position. Where many systems build longitudinal intelligence through primary care networks, India’s most complete clinical signals emerge from secondary facilities. These are not filtered or early-stage presentations. They are records of delay, escalation, and complexity \- often within the same patient journey. The difference is not cosmetic. It shapes what the system is able to see.

A significant proportion of healthcare data \- globally estimated at 60–80% \- exists in unstructured formats such as clinical notes, imaging, and reports (Raghupathi & Raghupathi, 2014; Li et al., 2021). In India, where digitization remains uneven, this proportion is likely higher. As illustrated in Figure 2, most clinical information is generated in forms that resist immediate analysis.

![][image2]

Figure 2: Distribution of structured versus unstructured healthcare data. Approximately 60–80% of healthcare data exists in unstructured formats, limiting its direct usability. Source: Raghupathi & Raghupathi (2014); Li et al. (2021).

The implication is not merely technical. A system that cannot structure its data cannot observe its own patterns. And a system that cannot observe patterns cannot anticipate demand, allocate resources efficiently, or intervene early in disease progression. At the level of primary care, the data that is captured tends to reflect early-stage conditions \- cases that enter the system before significant progression. This is necessary, but incomplete. It offers a view of disease at its onset, not at its consequence.

Secondary care presents a different picture. District hospitals in India routinely manage between 800 and 1,200 outpatient visits per day in high-volume settings (NHSRC, 2019). These facilities encounter not just onset, but accumulation \- conditions that have evolved over time, often without prior intervention. The resulting records are layered: diagnostics, prescriptions, follow-ups, and outcomes forming a longitudinal account of disease progression within a real-world context. This relationship is illustrated in Figure 3\.

![][image3]

Figure 3: Secondary care as the convergence point of patient volume and clinical data depth. Secondary facilities combine high patient volume with rich longitudinal clinical complexity. Source: Conceptual model informed by NHSRC (2019) and WHO (2022).

What Figure 2 makes visible is not just concentration, but convergence. Secondary care is the only layer where scale and complexity intersect \- where the volume of patients aligns with the depth of clinical information. And yet, this is also where the system’s informational potential begins to fragment. Despite large volumes of data being generated, estimates suggest that up to 80% remains underutilized due to lack of structuring, interoperability, and integration into decision-making processes (HIMSS, 2023). Figure 4 reflects this progressive loss.

![][image4]

Figure 4: Healthcare data utilization funnel. While most clinical data is generated, only a fraction is structured and an even smaller portion is used for decision-making. Source: HIMSS (2023); HealthTech Magazine (2023).

Each stage of loss is cumulative. By the time information reaches the point of decision-making, only a fraction of its original value remains. In simple terms, the constraint is not data generation \- it is data usability. India’s healthcare system is not constrained by the absence of data, but by its limited capacity to structure and interpret the data it already produces.

### **THE SOLUTION: AI AND WORKFLOW INTEGRATION**

Advances in artificial intelligence have begun to alter this equation. Natural language processing models can now extract structured information from unstructured clinical inputs \- handwritten notes, multilingual records, and fragmented reports \- at a scale previously unmanageable. What was once a collection of isolated records becomes, potentially, a linked and longitudinal dataset. The implication is not technological novelty, but systemic visibility. Patterns of disease emergence, treatment variation, and resource utilization become observable. The system shifts, gradually, from reacting to individual cases to recognizing trajectories across populations.

And yet, the transformation remains incomplete. The constraint is no longer capability, but integration. Healthcare environments operate under time and resource constraints that leave little room for additional processes. In secondary facilities, clinicians often manage 40–60 patients per day, compressing decision-making into minutes (MoHFW, 2022). Documentation is designed for immediacy, not for downstream analytics. What appears to be a technological gap is, in effect, a workflow misalignment.

Systems that require additional effort \- new interfaces, duplicate entry, or altered routines \- introduce friction. Adoption slows, not because of resistance, but because of feasibility. Even where digital systems exist, they often function as parallel layers rather than integrated ones, adding to administrative burden rather than reducing it. The consequences are visible but understated. For clinicians, each encounter begins with partial context. For nurses, documentation becomes repetitive. For patients, continuity depends as much on memory as on records. Information exists, but it does not accumulate.

### **THE ASYMMETRY: INVESTMENT VERSUS VALUE**

This misalignment is mirrored in how resources are distributed across the system. Investment in healthcare has traditionally followed visibility and specialization. Tertiary institutions attract capital due to advanced procedures and infrastructure requirements. Primary care remains central to policy design. Secondary care, positioned between the two, functions as a throughput layer \- absorbing demand without equivalent recognition as a site of strategic value creation. Figure 5 reflects this divergence.

![][image5]

Figure 5: Misalignment between investment allocation and data value generation across healthcare tiers. Secondary care generates the most representative clinical data but receives comparatively lower investment in data infrastructure. Source: National Health Accounts (India); World Bank (2022); WHO (2022).

The pattern is not accidental. The benefits of structured data \- improved resource allocation, early detection of disease patterns, and system-level efficiency \- are distributed across the system. The costs of implementing such systems, however, are borne locally at the facility level. This asymmetry slows adoption.

### **THE PATH FORWARD: CAPTURE, CONNECT, UTILIZE**

At the policy level, however, movement is visible. Initiatives such as the Ayushman Bharat Digital Health Mission are establishing foundational infrastructure \- unique health identifiers, federated data architecture, and consent-based exchange mechanisms (NHA, 2023). Disease-specific programs, including the National Cancer Registry Programme, demonstrate how aggregated clinical data can inform population-level strategy. The pieces are in place. What remains is alignment.

In simple terms, the transition from fragmented data to system intelligence follows three steps: capturing structured data at the point of care, connecting it across institutions, and embedding it into decision-making processes. Figure 6 reflects this progression.

![][image6]

Figure 6: Pathway from data generation to system intelligence through capture, connection, and utilization. Source: NHA (2023); WHO (2022); McKinsey (2023).

The sequence is not interchangeable. Without capture, there is nothing to connect. Without connection, there is nothing to utilize. Without utilization, the system does not change. The two patients who began their journeys differently did not encounter different systems. They encountered different entry points into the same system \- one as it was designed, and one as it is used. Over time, it is the latter that has come to define its center of gravity. What remains less visible is that it has also become the system’s most complete record of reality. The data already exists. The capability to structure it is emerging. The infrastructure to connect it is being built. What follows is a quieter question. Whether the system will recognize where its most complete picture already resides \- and choose to build around it.

**References**

* Raghupathi, W., & Raghupathi, V. (2014). Big Data Analytics in Healthcare: Promise and Potential. Health Information Science and Systems.  
* Li, I., et al. (2021). Unstructured Data in Healthcare: Challenges and Opportunities. Journal of Medical Systems.  
* World Health Organization (WHO). (2022). Digital Health and Health Systems Strengthening.  
* National Health Systems Resource Centre (NHSRC). (2019). Healthcare Utilization Patterns in India.  
* Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW). (2022). Rural Health Statistics.  
* National Health Authority (NHA). (2023). Ayushman Bharat Digital Health Mission Framework.  
* World Bank. (2022). Health Financing in India.  
* HIMSS. (2023). Healthcare Data Utilization Reports.  
* HealthTech Magazine. (2023). Structured vs Unstructured Data in Healthcare.  
* McKinsey & Company. (2023). Digital Health and AI Reports.

`,(0,t.jsxDEV)(n.p,{children:"The implication is not merely technical. A system that cannot structure its data cannot observe its own patterns. `,(0,t.jsxDEV)(n.h3,{children:(0,t.jsxDEV)(n.strong,{children:"THE SOLUTION: AI AND WORKFLOW INTEGRATION"},void 0,!1,{fileName:"D:\\MONOVERSE\\content\\essays\\_mdx_bundler_entry_point-f93861e5-f357-416b-8ffb-e06e894489a7.mdx",lineNumber:58,columnNumber:5},this)},void 0,!1,{fileName:"D:\\MONOVERSE\\content\\essays\\_mdx_bundler_entry_point-f93861e5-f357-416b-8ffb-e06e894489a7.mdx",lineNumber:58,columnNumber:1},this),`
`,(0,t.jsxDEV)(n.p,{children:"Advances in artificial intelligence have begun to alter this equation. Natural language processing models can now extract structured information from unstructured clinical inputs - handwritten notes, multilingual records, and fragmented reports - at a scale previously unmanageable. What was once a collection of isolated records becomes, potentially, a linked and longitudinal dataset. The implication is not technological novelty, but systemic visibility. Patterns of disease emergence, treatment variation, and resource utilization become observable. The system shifts, gradually, from reacting to individual cases to recognizing trajectories across populations."},void 0,!1,{fileName:"D:\\MONOVERSE\\content\\essays\\_mdx_bundler_entry_point-f93861e5-f357-416b-8ffb-e06e894489a7.mdx",lineNumber:60,columnNumber:1},this),`
`,(0,t.jsxDEV)(n.p,{children:"And yet, the transformation remains incomplete. The constraint is no longer capability, but integration. Healthcare environments operate under time and resource constraints that leave little room for additional processes. In secondary facilities, clinicians often manage 40\u201360 patients per day, compressing decision-making into minutes (MoHFW, 2022). Documentation is designed for immediacy, not for downstream analytics. What appears to be a technological gap is, in effect, a workflow misalignment."},void 0,!1,{fileName:"D:\\MONOVERSE\\content\\essays\\_mdx_bundler_entry_point-f93861e5-f357-416b-8ffb-e06e894489a7.mdx",lineNumber:62,columnNumber:1},this),`
`,(0,t.jsxDEV)(n.p,{children:"Systems that require additional effort - new interfaces, duplicate entry, or altered routines - introduce friction. Adoption slows, not because of resistance, but because of feasibility. Even where digital systems exist, they often function as parallel layers rather than integrated ones, adding to administrative burden rather than reducing it. The consequences are visible but understated. For clinicians, each encounter begins with partial context. For nurses, documentation becomes repetitive. For patients, continuity depends as much on memory as on records. Information exists, but it does not accumulate."},void 0,!1,{fileName:"D:\\MONOVERSE\\content\\essays\\_mdx_bundler_entry_point-f93861e5-f357-416b-8ffb-e06e894489a7.mdx",lineNumber:64,columnNumber:1},this),`

`,(0,t.jsxDEV)(n.p,{children:"The sequence is not interchangeable. Without capture, there is nothing to connect. Without connection, there is nothing to utilize. Without utilization, the system does not change. The two patients who began their journeys differently did not encounter different systems. They encountered different entry points into the same system - one as it was designed, and one as it is used. Over time, it is the latter that has come to define its center of gravity. What remains less visible is that it has also become the system\u2019s most complete record of reality. The data already exists. The capability to structure it is emerging. The infrastructure to connect it is being built. What follows is a quieter question. Whether the system will recognize where its most complete picture already resides - and choose to build around it."},void 0,!1,{fileName:"D:\\MONOVERSE\\content\\essays\\_mdx_bundler_entry_point-f93861e5-f357-416b-8ffb-e06e894489a7.mdx",lineNumber:86,columnNumber:1},this),`
